
## 7.5-minute recording with a falling heart rate

### Test your predictions using the dataset

The recording comes from an Aidlab chest strap (MIT licence). It lasts 450 s and
contains ECG, beat-to-beat RR intervals, a 5-s pulse signal, respiration,
3-axis acceleration and body position. All timestamps are Unix milliseconds
(UTC). We express time in seconds from the start of the recording
(`from_timestamp_ms` in `dataset.json`).

#### Data import and preparation

An **RR interval** is the time, in milliseconds, between two successive
heartbeats (two successive R waves of the ECG). Heart rate in beats per minute
is obtained by dividing one minute (60 000 ms) by this interval:

$$HR = \frac{60\,000}{RR}$$

For example, an RR interval of 400 ms corresponds to 150 bpm.

We use the RR intervals as the **main signal**, because each heartbeat gives one
HR value: about 1 000 points over the recording. The device's `pulse` signal
gives only one HR value about every 5 s (91 values), so it describes the
recovery curve much less precisely. We keep `pulse` as an **independent
cross-check** of the RR-derived HR. We also import the **acceleration**, to find
out when the participant is moving, because movement keeps HR high and
therefore affects the recovery curve.

```{r}
#| label: r7-import

# Folder containing the 7.5-min recording
r7_dir <- "data/cardio-recovery-7m30s"

# Read the metadata to get the exact start time of the recording
r7_meta <- jsonlite::read_json(file.path(r7_dir, "dataset.json"))
r7_t0 <- r7_meta$from_timestamp_ms   # start time (Unix ms)

# Beat-to-beat heart rate from RR intervals
r7_rr <- read_csv(file.path(r7_dir, "rr.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(t = (timestamp - r7_t0) / 1000,   # time from start, in seconds
         rr = value,                       # RR interval, in ms
         hr = 60000 / rr)                  # heart rate, in bpm

# Device heart rate (one value every ~5 s), used as a cross-check
r7_pulse <- read_csv(file.path(r7_dir, "pulse.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(t = (timestamp - r7_t0) / 1000,   # time from start, in seconds
         hr = value)                       # heart rate, in bpm

# Acceleration: one row per sample, with x, y and z in g
r7_acc <- read_csv(file.path(r7_dir, "acceleration.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(t = (timestamp - r7_t0) / 1000,          # time from start, in seconds
         mag = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)) |>          # magnitude of the 3-axis vector
  group_by(t = floor(t / 10) * 10 + 5) |>         # 10-s windows, centred
  summarise(acc_sd = sd(mag), .groups = "drop")   # movement = SD within window

# Summary of the signals used
tibble(signal = c("RR intervals", "pulse", "acceleration (10-s windows)"),
       n = c(nrow(r7_rr), nrow(r7_pulse), nrow(r7_acc)),
       t_start_s = c(min(r7_rr$t), min(r7_pulse$t), min(r7_acc$t)),
       t_end_s = c(max(r7_rr$t), max(r7_pulse$t), max(r7_acc$t))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Signals used in the analysis")
```

Before fitting anything, we check the RR intervals for artefacts (missed or
extra beats). A common rule is to reject any interval that differs by more than
20 % from the previous one.

```{r}
#| label: r7-artefacts

# Flag RR intervals that differ by more than 20 % from the previous interval
r7_rr <- r7_rr |>
  mutate(rel_change = abs(rr / lag(rr) - 1),   # relative change vs previous beat
         artefact = !is.na(rel_change) & rel_change > 0.20)

r7_rr |>
  summarise(n_beats = n(),
            n_artefacts = sum(artefact),
            rr_min_ms = min(rr), rr_max_ms = max(rr),
            hr_min_bpm = min(hr), hr_max_bpm = max(hr)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "RR interval quality check")

r7_rr <- filter(r7_rr, !artefact)
```

No interval was rejected, so the RR series is clean. All RR values stay between
368 and 520 ms (115–163 bpm), which is physiologically plausible.

#### Identifying the exercise and recovery periods

```{r}
#| label: fig-r7-overview
#| fig-cap: "7.5-min recording. Top: beat-to-beat HR from RR intervals (grey) and device pulse (black). Bottom: movement (SD of acceleration magnitude, 10-s windows). The dashed line at 330 s marks the moment the participant stops moving."
#| fig-height: 6

# Time at which the participant stops moving (read from the acceleration plot)
r7_t_still <- 330

# Top panel: heart rate from RR (points) and from the device pulse (line)
r7_p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = r7_rr, aes(t, hr), colour = "grey60", size = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = r7_pulse, aes(t, hr), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = r7_t_still, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Heart rate (bpm)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Bottom panel: movement index (SD of acceleration magnitude)
r7_p2 <- ggplot(r7_acc, aes(t, acc_sd)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = r7_t_still, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Time from start of recording (s)", y = "Acceleration SD (g)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Stack the two panels
patchwork::wrap_plots(r7_p1, r7_p2, ncol = 1, heights = c(2, 1))
```

What we observe:

- **No exercise period is visible.** HR is already about 155 bpm in the first
  seconds and starts falling right away. The exercise ended **before** the
  recording started, and we do not know exactly when. So $t = 0$ is the start of
  the recording, not the end of exercise.
- **Fast phase (≈ 0–90 s):** HR drops from about 155 to 131 bpm while the
  participant is moving (acceleration SD ≈ 0.2–0.27 g, a level consistent with
  light activity such as walking).
- **Short pause (≈ 80–100 s):** movement stops briefly (SD ≈ 0.02 g) and HR
  reaches a local minimum (~131 bpm).
- **Plateau (≈ 100–330 s):** movement starts again and HR stays around
  130–137 bpm instead of continuing to fall. This is an **active recovery**.
  The small HR rise around 240–290 s happens while the participant is moving.
- **Rest (≈ 330–450 s):** movement almost stops (SD < 0.07 g) and HR drops
  again, to about 124–130 bpm.
- The body position signal only contains the label `unknown`, so it does not
  help.
  
We therefore consider the **whole recording (0–450 s) as the post-exercise
recovery period**. However, the activity is not constant: it changes from
active to passive recovery at about 330 s. No decay model contains this change,
so we also fit the models on the active part only (0–330 s) as a sensitivity
analysis.

Because $t = 0$ is not the end of exercise, the amplitude of an exponential is
not the true HR drop since the end of exercise. The time constant $\tau$ is not
affected, though: shifting time by $\delta$ in
$a\,e^{-(t+\delta)/\tau}$ only multiplies the amplitude by $e^{-\delta/\tau}$.
Only $\tau$ can be compared with the literature.
#### Fitting the models

We fit the three required models to the beat-to-beat HR:

- **Linear:** $HR(t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t$
- **Mono-exponential:** $HR(t) = HR_\infty + a\,e^{-t/\tau}$
- **Bi-exponential:** $HR(t) = HR_\infty + a_1 e^{-t/\tau_1} + a_2 e^{-t/\tau_2}$

Non-linear models are fitted by least squares with `nls()`. The bi-exponential
is sensitive to starting values, so we try several and keep the best converged
fit. We use the `port` algorithm with bounds ($a_i \ge 0$, $\tau_i \ge 1$ s).

```{r}
#| label: r7-fit-functions

# Fit a bi-exponential from several starting points and keep the best one
r7_fit_biexp <- function(d) {
  # Three sets of starting values (see text)
  starts <- list(
    list(hr_inf = 125, a1 = 25, tau1 = 40, a2 = 5,  tau2 = 150),
    list(hr_inf = 110, a1 = 25, tau1 = 50, a2 = 25, tau2 = 1000),
    list(hr_inf = 120, a1 = 20, tau1 = 30, a2 = 10, tau2 = 400)
  )
  # Try each set; return NULL instead of stopping if the fit fails
  fits <- map(starts, \(s) tryCatch(
    nls(hr ~ hr_inf + a1 * exp(-t / tau1) + a2 * exp(-t / tau2),
        data = d, start = s, algorithm = "port",
        lower = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 1),           # bounds: hr_inf, a1, tau1, a2, tau2
        upper = c(200, 200, 1e4, 200, 1e5),
        control = list(maxiter = 500)),
    error = function(e) NULL))
  fits <- compact(fits)                     # drop the failed fits
  if (length(fits) == 0) return(NULL)       # no fit converged
  fits[[which.min(map_dbl(fits, deviance))]] # best fit = smallest residual SS
}

# Fit the three models to a data set with columns t and hr
r7_fit_models <- function(d) {
  list(
    linear = lm(hr ~ t, data = d),
    mono = nls(hr ~ hr_inf + a * exp(-t / tau), data = d,
               start = list(hr_inf = 130, a = 25, tau = 40)),
    bi = r7_fit_biexp(d)
  )
}

# Goodness-of-fit and residual indicators for a list of models
r7_indicators <- function(models, d) {
  imap(compact(models), \(m, name) {
    e <- resid(m)                                      # residuals
    tibble(model = name,
           k = length(coef(m)),                        # number of parameters
           RMSE = sqrt(mean(e^2)),                     # typical error (bpm)
           R2 = 1 - sum(e^2) / sum((d$hr - mean(d$hr))^2), # explained variance
           AIC = AIC(m),
           BIC = BIC(m),
           DW = sum(diff(e)^2) / sum(e^2),             # Durbin-Watson
           acf_lag1 = acf(e, plot = FALSE)$acf[2],     # lag-1 autocorrelation
           LjungBox_p = Box.test(e, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(dAIC = AIC - min(AIC), .after = AIC)        # difference to best AIC
}
```

```{r}
#| label: r7-fit-full

# Fit the three models on the whole recording
r7_models <- r7_fit_models(r7_rr)

# Compute and display the indicators
r7_ind <- r7_indicators(r7_models, r7_rr)

knitr::kable(r7_ind, digits = c(0, 0, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3),
             caption = "Model comparison on the whole recording (0–450 s, beat-to-beat HR)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-r7-fits
#| fig-cap: "Linear, mono-exponential and bi-exponential fits to the beat-to-beat heart rate (whole recording)."

# Predictions of each model on a 1-s time grid
r7_grid <- tibble(t = seq(0, max(r7_rr$t), by = 1))
r7_pred <- imap(compact(r7_models), \(m, name)
                mutate(r7_grid, model = name, hr = predict(m, newdata = r7_grid))) |>
  list_rbind()

# Data (grey points) and fitted curves (coloured lines)
ggplot(r7_rr, aes(t, hr)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey70", size = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = r7_pred, aes(colour = model), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = r7_t_still, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Time from start of recording (s)", y = "Heart rate (bpm)",
       colour = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### Fitted parameters

```{r}
#| label: r7-params

# Table of estimates, standard errors and Wald 95 % CI for one model
r7_param_table <- function(m, name) {
  s <- summary(m)$coefficients
  tibble(model = name, parameter = rownames(s),
         estimate = s[, 1], SE = s[, 2],
         CI_low = s[, 1] - 1.96 * s[, 2],
         CI_high = s[, 1] + 1.96 * s[, 2])
}

imap(compact(r7_models), r7_param_table) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Fitted parameters (Wald 95 % CI, whole recording)")
```

- **Linear:** HR falls by `r round(-coef(r7_models$linear)["t"] * 60, 1)`
  bpm/min on average. This model has no physiological meaning: it would predict
  HR to keep falling indefinitely, which is impossible.
  - **Mono-exponential:** $\tau =$ `r round(coef(r7_models$mono)["tau"], 1)` s and
  $HR_\infty =$ `r round(coef(r7_models$mono)["hr_inf"], 1)` bpm. All
  parameters are precise and physiologically interpretable: HR tends towards
  about 131 bpm, the level kept up by the active recovery.
  - **Bi-exponential:** the fast component
  ($\tau_1 \approx$ `r round(coef(r7_models$bi)["tau1"], 1)` s) is plausible,
  but the slow component is **not**:
  $\tau_2 \approx$ `r round(coef(r7_models$bi)["tau2"])` s (more than 2 hours,
  much longer than the 7.5-min recording),
  $a_2 \approx$ `r round(coef(r7_models$bi)["a2"])` bpm, and
  $HR_\infty \approx$ `r round(coef(r7_models$bi)["hr_inf"])` bpm, stuck at the
  lower bound. When $\tau_2 \gg t$, $a_2 e^{-t/\tau_2} \approx a_2 - (a_2/\tau_2)\,t$.
  The "slow exponential" is just a **straight line** with slope
  `r round(-coef(r7_models$bi)["a2"] / coef(r7_models$bi)["tau2"] * 60, 2)`
  bpm/min. $HR_\infty$, $a_2$ and $\tau_2$ cannot be estimated separately (the
  model is not identifiable here), which is also why their standard errors are
  so large.

The data therefore do not contain a second exponential phase within 450 s. What
the bi-exponential captures is a slow downward **drift**, caused mainly by the
end of movement at 330 s. To check this, we fit a more parsimonious model with
the same shape, a **mono-exponential plus a linear drift** (4 parameters instead
of 5):

$$HR(t) = HR_0 + a\,e^{-t/\tau} + b\,t$$


```{r}
#| label: r7-drift

# Mono-exponential + linear drift (b = slope of the drift, bpm/s)
r7_drift <- nls(hr ~ hr0 + a * exp(-t / tau) + b * t, data = r7_rr,
                start = list(hr0 = 130, a = 25, tau = 40, b = 0))

r7_param_table(r7_drift, "mono + drift") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Mono-exponential + linear drift")

r7_indicators(c(compact(r7_models), list(`mono + drift` = r7_drift)), r7_rr) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3),
               caption = "Comparison including the mono-exponential + drift model")
```

The mono-exponential + drift reproduces the bi-exponential: same fast time
constant ($\tau \approx$ `r round(coef(r7_drift)["tau"], 1)` s), same slope.
It has one parameter less and a lower AIC and BIC. This confirms that the
"second phase" of the bi-exponential is a linear trend and not a second
recovery process.

Nested models (mono-exponential vs bi-exponential) can also be compared with an
extra-sum-of-squares F-test:

```{r}
#| label: r7-ftest

# Does adding the second exponential reduce the residual SS significantly?
anova(r7_models$mono, r7_models$bi)
```

The F-test is highly significant, but this is not enough to choose the
bi-exponential: its extra parameters are not interpretable, and the residuals
are strongly autocorrelated (next section). This violates the independence
assumption that the F-test and the standard errors rely on, so their p-values
are far too optimistic.

#### Residual analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-r7-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals of each model versus time (whole recording). Blue line: LOESS smooth. A good model should leave residuals randomly scattered around 0."
#| fig-height: 6

# Residuals of the four models in one long table
r7_res <- imap(c(compact(r7_models), list(`mono + drift` = r7_drift)),
               \(m, name) tibble(model = name, t = r7_rr$t, resid = resid(m))) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model))   # keep the models in this order

# Residuals vs time, one panel per model, with a smooth trend line
ggplot(r7_res, aes(t, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.2, se = FALSE, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = r7_t_still, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time from start of recording (s)", y = "Residual (bpm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-r7-acf
#| fig-cap: "Autocorrelation of the residuals (lags in beats). Dashed lines: approximate 95 % bounds for white noise."
#| fig-height: 3.5

# Autocorrelation function of the residuals (lags 0 to 30 beats) for each model
r7_res |>
  group_by(model) |>
  reframe(lag = 0:30, acf = acf(resid, lag.max = 30, plot = FALSE)$acf[, 1, 1]) |>
  ggplot(aes(lag, acf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  # 95 % bounds expected if the residuals were white noise
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(r7_rr)), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0)) +
  facet_wrap(~model, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Lag (beats)", y = "ACF") +
  theme_minimal()
```

- **Linear:** residuals show a clear U-shaped pattern: positive at the start,
  negative in the middle, positive again. The model misses the curvature of the
  fast phase. This is a systematic error, not noise.
- **Mono-exponential:** the fast phase is captured well, but the residuals
  become negative after 330 s, when the participant stops moving and HR drops
  below the predicted plateau. There is also a negative dip around 100 s, which
  matches the short pause in movement.
- **Bi-exponential / mono + drift:** the end-of-recording trend is partly
  absorbed, but slow waves remain (for example around 240–290 s, a period of
  movement).
- **For all models**, residuals stay strongly autocorrelated (lag-1 ACF ≈ 0.7,
  Durbin-Watson ≪ 2, Ljung-Box p ≈ 0). Part of this comes from the physiology:
  beat-to-beat HR oscillates with breathing (respiratory sinus arrhythmia) and
  with changes in movement. No smooth decay curve can capture this. As a
  result, the AIC, standard errors and F-test computed on ~1 000 beats overstate
  the evidence. The differences between models should be read as indicative.
  #### Sensitivity analyses

We check whether the conclusions depend on our choices: (1) fitting only the
**active-recovery window** (0–330 s, constant activity), (2) using the device's
**pulse** signal instead of RR, and (3) averaging RR-derived HR into **5-s bins**
to reduce beat-to-beat noise and autocorrelation.

```{r}
#| label: r7-sensitivity

# Data sets for the sensitivity analysis
r7_active <- filter(r7_rr, t <= r7_t_still)      # active recovery only
r7_bins <- r7_rr |>                               # RR-derived HR averaged in 5-s bins
  group_by(t = floor(t / 5) * 5 + 2.5) |>
  summarise(hr = mean(hr), .groups = "drop")

r7_sens <- list(
  "RR, 0–450 s (main)" = r7_rr,
  "RR, 0–330 s (active only)" = r7_active,
  "Pulse, 0–450 s" = r7_pulse,
  "RR 5-s bins, 0–450 s" = r7_bins
)

# Refit the three models on each data set and keep the key results
r7_sens_tab <- imap(r7_sens, \(d, name) {
  ms <- r7_fit_models(d)
  ind <- r7_indicators(ms, d)
  tibble(dataset = name,
         n = nrow(d),
         tau_mono = coef(ms$mono)["tau"],
         tau_CI = paste0("[", paste(round(coef(ms$mono)["tau"] + c(-1.96, 1.96) *
                          summary(ms$mono)$coefficients["tau", 2], 1), collapse = "; "), "]"),
         hr_inf_mono = coef(ms$mono)["hr_inf"],
         dAIC_linear = ind$dAIC[ind$model == "linear"] - ind$dAIC[ind$model == "mono"],
         bi_converged = !is.null(ms$bi),
         tau2_bi = if (is.null(ms$bi)) NA_real_ else coef(ms$bi)["tau2"])
}) |>
  list_rbind()

knitr::kable(r7_sens_tab, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Data", "n", "τ mono (s)", "95 % CI", "HR∞ mono (bpm)",
                           "AIC linear − AIC mono", "Bi-exp converged?", "τ₂ bi-exp (s)"),
             caption = "Sensitivity of the results to the data and window used")
```

- The **mono-exponential time constant is robust to the signal**: about
  63–65 s on the whole recording, whether we use RR, pulse or 5-s bins. It
  **does depend on the window**. On the active window only it is shorter
  (≈ 49 s), close to the value obtained with the drift term (≈ 44 s). On the
  whole recording, the end-of-movement drop pulls the curve down and makes the
  exponential look slower than it is.
- The mono-exponential always beats the linear model by a large AIC margin.
- When the activity is constant (0–330 s), **the bi-exponential cannot be
  fitted at all**: there is no second exponential phase to estimate. Whenever it
  does converge, its slow component degenerates into a linear drift
  ($\tau_2$ of several thousand seconds).
  
#### Summary of findings for this recording

- The recording covers **recovery only**: exercise ended shortly before it
  started. The recovery is **active** until ~330 s (participant moving), then
  **passive**.
- The **linear model** is clearly rejected: worst fit, systematic curvature in
  the residuals, and no physiological meaning.
- The **mono-exponential model** is the best compromise. With only 3
  parameters it explains most of the variance and gives an interpretable time
  constant and a plateau (~131–133 bpm) that matches the HR kept up by ongoing
  movement. Its best estimate is the one obtained on a window of constant
  activity: **$\tau \approx 49$ s** (95 % CI ≈ 44–53 s, 0–330 s). On the whole
  recording $\tau \approx 63$ s, which is biased upwards by the late drop.
- The **mono-exponential + linear drift** has the lowest AIC/BIC on the whole
  recording, but its drift term is purely empirical: a straight line cannot
  continue forever. It is useful to show that the bi-exponential's "slow
  phase" is only a trend, not as a physiological model.
- The **bi-exponential model is not justified** here. Its slightly better
  statistics come from a slow component that is mathematically a straight line
  and physiologically meaningless ($\tau_2$ > 2 h). It cannot be fitted when the
  activity is constant. A 7.5-min recording is too short to identify a true slow
  recovery phase, which would need tens of minutes of data.
- The **remaining structure** in the residuals (late drop, mid-recording wave,
  autocorrelation) comes from **changes in physical activity and breathing**,
  not from the decay law itself. Any HRR model applied to this recording should
  account for the activity state (for example by fitting active and passive
  phases separately).
